findings.claim: Five descriptions are cut off mid-sentence with a full stop bolted on, e.g. L2 'and the gap between the.', L3 'the first Parliament with elected.', L4 "broken promises sparked England's.", L8 'and how Parliament finally.', L10 'how working people built.'
findings.truth: Each was truncated at the 100-character cap during the build. Rewritten to complete sentences under 100 characters (lessons 2, 3, 4, 8, 10).
findings.evidence: raw description fields; validator limit of 100 characters

findings.claim: The unit teaches the wrong question set for Paper 2 Section A throughout: 'The four question types: 4-mark two ways similar or different, 8-mark explain the significance, 8-mark explain a development, and 16-mark factors essay.' 25 practice questions are tariffed at 4 marks and 16 are 'Explain a Development'. No source question appears anywhere.
findings.truth: The spec's assessment section sets four compulsory questions worth 40 marks plus 4 SPaG: Q1 'How useful is source...' (8, AO3, visual or written source), Q2 'Explain the significance of...' (8), Q3 'Explain two ways in which X and Y were similar/different' (8), Q4 factors essay (16 + 4 SPaG). There is no 'explain a development' question on this paper and the comparison is 8 marks, not 4. All 41 mis-set questions converted to real forms with rebuilt mark schemes; the four types corrected in lesson 1 content, conclusion, exam tip and flashcards, and in the exam tips of lessons 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A question table and notes on questions 1-4; spec 2.2 (Paper 2: 2 hours, 84 marks, Section A four compulsory questions, 40 marks plus 4 SPaG)

findings.claim: Fifteen invented exam claims across lessons 1, 2, 5, 6, 9 and 14, including 'Examiner reports warn that students who present individuals ... lose marks', 'Examiner reports flag this repeatedly', 'The lesson AQA wants you to draw', 'examiners reward genuinely distinct points', 'the mark scheme rewards ...', 'Examiner reports flag four recurring problems', and a flashcard citing 'the AO2 analytical-link descriptors'.
findings.truth: None of these can be sourced to the specification and no examiner report is quoted. Reworded as plain teaching advice, keeping only what the spec itself states (that the role of the individual is one of the listed factors, and that SPaG rewards specialist terms).
findings.evidence: spec 3.3.1 factor list and 4.4.3 SPaG criteria; no examiner-report source in the unit

findings.claim: 'The Pope put England under an interdict from 1208 to 1213' (and the same dates in a knowledge-check match set).
findings.truth: The interdict ran from March 1208 to July 1214. John submitted in May 1213 and his excommunication was lifted that year, but the interdict itself was not raised until 1214.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Interdict (Catholic canon law)': England under interdict 'for six years between March 1208 and July 1214'

findings.claim: 'The 1297 version remains technically in force today - clause 39 is still UK law'; a flashcard says 'Clause 39 of the 1297 reissue is still on the statute book'; a mark scheme calls it 'the only medieval text on the modern statute book'.
findings.truth: Three clauses of the 1297 statute survive, and the due-process clause is numbered 29 there (clause 39 of the 1215 charter). It is not the only surviving medieval statute; the Statute of Marlborough 1267 is older and still partly in force. Reworded to 'renumbered 29' and 'among the oldest law still on the statute book'.
findings.evidence: 1297 Magna Carta statute numbering; UK statute book

findings.claim: 'On 13 June, Tyler's men crossed London Bridge ... They opened prisons, killing Flemish merchants in Cheapside, and stormed the Tower of London - dragging out and beheading the Archbishop of Canterbury Simon Sudbury ... and the Treasurer Robert Hales.' The Mile End meeting is then given as the next day.
findings.truth: The Savoy was burned on the evening of 13 June, but the Tower was stormed on 14 June while Richard II was at Mile End, and Sudbury and Hales were beheaded on Tower Hill that day. The killing of Flemish merchants also belongs to 14 June. Sequence corrected across the two paragraphs.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Peasants' Revolt' day-by-day sequence for 13-15 June 1381

findings.claim: 'Around 150 rebels were executed in total' (repeated as 'around 150 in 1381' in a lesson 5 comparison mark scheme).
findings.truth: By November 1381 at least 1,500 rebels had been executed or killed in the reprisals. The lesson 5 comparison bullet, which used the 150 figure to argue Henry VIII was 'more systematic', has been rewritten so the contrast still holds.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Peasants' Revolt': 'by November at least 1,500 people had been executed or killed in battle'

findings.claim: 'the pattern that will recur with the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1537'.
findings.truth: The Pilgrimage of Grace was October to December 1536; Bigod's rising, the broken pardon and the executions followed in 1537. The spec names it under Part two without a date, and the rest of the unit dates it 1536.
findings.evidence: spec 3.3.1 Part two; lesson 5 of this unit

findings.claim: 'Later northern risings (the Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549, the Northern Earls of 1569) framed themselves more cautiously and were crushed faster.'
findings.truth: The Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549 was in Devon and Cornwall, not the north, and it was not cautious. Reworded to 'Later religious risings (the Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549 in the West Country, the Northern Earls of 1569) were smaller and were crushed faster.'
findings.evidence: Prayer Book (Western) Rebellion 1549, Devon and Cornwall

findings.claim: 'their text survived and became a touchstone of British radicalism: even Chartists in the 1830s and 40s explicitly cited Rainsborough', with 'Chartists, suffragettes and modern democrats all traced their language back to Putney' and the same claim in a significance mark scheme.
findings.truth: The shorthand record of the Putney Debates (the Clarke Papers) was lost until it was rediscovered at Worcester College, Oxford in 1890. No Chartist could have read or cited it. Corrected in all three places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Putney Debates': the transcripts were rediscovered in 1890 at Worcester College, Oxford

findings.claim: 'Britain had a smaller population than the colonies, an over-stretched navy, and supply lines 3,000 miles long.'
findings.truth: Great Britain had roughly 8 million people in 1775; the thirteen colonies had about 2.4 million. Britain's population was about three times larger. The navy and the 3,000-mile supply line are correct.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Thirteen Colonies': colonial population about 2.4 million in 1775

findings.claim: 'In November 1839 around 5,000 South Wales miners marched on Newport, hoping to free imprisoned Chartist John Frost.'
findings.truth: John Frost led the march. He was a former mayor of Newport, not a prisoner. The marchers were trying to free Chartist prisoners held in the town, and the wider aim was the release of Henry Vincent.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Newport Rising': led by John Frost, Zephaniah Williams and William Jones; the marchers aimed to liberate Chartists held at the Westgate Hotel

findings.claim: 'five of the six demands eventually became law - the secret ballot in 1872, votes for working men in 1867 and 1884, paid MPs in 1911, and universal manhood suffrage in 1918.'
findings.truth: That list names only three distinct points (manhood suffrage is counted twice). The missing two are the abolition of the property qualification for MPs in 1858 - the date in the lesson's own title, which the lesson never explained - and roughly equal constituencies from 1885. Both added.
findings.evidence: six points of the People's Charter 1838; Property Qualification for Members of Parliament Act 1858; Redistribution of Seats Act 1885

findings.claim: 'Hannah More and the female anti-slavery societies ran the sugar boycott' of 1791.
findings.truth: Women were central to the 1791-92 abstention campaign, but organised female anti-slavery societies date from the 1820s (Birmingham 1825), thirty years later. Reworded to credit women campaigners in 1791 and place the societies in the 1820s.
findings.evidence: first Ladies' anti-slavery society, Birmingham 1825; sugar boycott 1791-92

findings.claim: 'Peel told the Commons it was the League's campaign, more than any single MP, that had moved him.'
findings.truth: The opposite. In his resignation speech of June 1846 Peel singled out one man by name, saying the name that ought to be associated with the success of the measure was that of Richard Cobden.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Richard Cobden': Peel's June 1846 resignation speech credited Cobden 'more than anyone else' with repeal

findings.claim: 'In June 1888 around 1,400 women and girls walked out of the Bryant & May factory ... After three weeks the company conceded.'
findings.truth: Annie Besant's article in The Link appeared on 23 June 1888, but the walkout followed a dismissal on about 2 July and the whole factory had stopped by 6 July. Terms were agreed on 16 July - about two weeks, not three.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'London matchgirls strike of 1888': article 23 June, walkout early July, settlement 16 July

findings.claim: 'The electorate quadrupled to over 21 million' - repeated in the key fact, in the glossary definition, inside the dfn data-def attribute, and in a lesson 14 mark scheme.
findings.truth: The electorate rose from about 7.7 million to 21.4 million: it almost tripled. Corrected in all five places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Representation of the People Act 1918': 7.7 million entitled to vote in 1912; 21.4 million by the end of 1918, a nearly threefold increase

findings.claim: 'the under-representation of women in Parliament (still under 35 per cent in 2024)'.
findings.truth: 34 per cent was the figure after the 2019 election. The 2024 election returned a record number of women, just over 40 per cent of the Commons.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Women in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom': 220 women (34 per cent) in 2019; an all-time high of 41 per cent after 2024

findings.claim: "Christabel Pankhurst's newspaper Votes for Women" (also in a lesson 14 mark scheme).
findings.truth: Votes for Women was founded and edited by Frederick and Emmeline Pethick-Lawrence. After the 1912 split the WSPU launched The Suffragette, which Christabel Pankhurst edited.
findings.evidence: WSPU press history: Votes for Women (Pethick-Lawrences, 1907); The Suffragette (Christabel Pankhurst, 1912)

findings.claim: 'The 1982 Act allowed employers to sue unions for unlawful strikes and ended the closed shop' (also in the key fact, the conclusion and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The Employment Act 1982 made closed shops conditional on periodic ballots and made most dismissals for non-membership unfair; the closed shop was not abolished until the Employment Acts of 1988 and 1990. Reworded to 'tightly restricted'.
findings.evidence: Employment Act 1982; Employment Act 1988; Employment Act 1990

findings.claim: 'In June 1948 the troopship Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury ... Earlier that year Parliament had passed the British Nationality Act.'
findings.truth: The Act received Royal Assent on 30 July 1948, six weeks after the Windrush docked, and came into force on 1 January 1949. The passengers travelled as British subjects under the law as it already stood.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'British Nationality Act 1948': Royal Assent 30 July 1948, in force 1 January 1949

findings.claim: 'Around 300 police officers and 65 civilians were injured' in the 1981 Brixton riot - repeated in the dfn data-def, the glossary, the exam tip, two mark schemes and a flashcard.
findings.truth: 279 police officers and 45 members of the public were injured. The 28 burned buildings and the absence of deaths are correct. Corrected in all six places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1981 Brixton riot': 279 injuries to police and 45 injuries to members of the public; 28 premises burned

findings.claim: 'On 22 April 1993 a 19-year-old Black sixth-former, Stephen Lawrence, was murdered'.
findings.truth: Stephen Lawrence was born on 13 September 1974 and was 18 when he was murdered.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Murder of Stephen Lawrence': born 13 September 1974, aged 18 at his death

findings.claim: 'War is decisive at specific moments: 1215 (Bouvines), 1642-51 (Civil War), 1914-18 (women's suffrage).'
findings.truth: Bouvines was fought on 27 July 1214. 1215 is the year of Magna Carta, which lesson 2 dates correctly.
findings.evidence: Battle of Bouvines, 27 July 1214

findings.claim: 'The 16-mark factors essay is marked against three Assessment Objectives', then only two are listed.
findings.truth: Question 4 of Section A tests AO1 and AO2 only, with 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A question table: question 4 carries AO1 6, AO2 10 and SPaG 4

findings.claim: 'The plan turns a 50-minute essay into a structured argument rather than a story.'
findings.truth: Paper 2 allows 2 hours for 84 marks across two equally weighted sections. The 16-mark essay plus its 4 SPaG marks is worth about 25 minutes, not 50.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Paper 2: written exam 2 hours, 84 marks, Sections A and B equally weighted

findings.claim: Seven flashcard answers are comma lists, which the validator rejects: e.g. 'War, religion, chance, government, communication, the economy, and ideas.', 'Window-smashing, arson, and hunger strikes.', 'Franchise, parliamentary supremacy, mass movement.'
findings.truth: Rewritten to one idea per card, with the question adjusted to match (lessons 1, 4, 6, 11, 14).
findings.evidence: checker brief flashcard rules; validator limits

findings.claim: Five flashcard answers are a single token: '1832.', '1838.', '1807.', '1824-25.', 'Religion.'
findings.truth: Each answer extended to a few words that carry a fact, keeping the question stem.
findings.evidence: checker brief flashcard rules

findings.claim: "both ended with the removal of a Stuart-line king's authority - Charles I executed 1649, George III's authority rejected over the colonies in 1776."
findings.truth: George III was a Hanoverian. Reworded to 'both ended with a king's authority destroyed by his own subjects'.
findings.evidence: House of Hanover from 1714

findings.claim: 'basis of due process and habeas corpus; cited in the US Constitution and modern human rights debates.'
findings.truth: Magna Carta influenced American constitutional language but is not cited in the US Constitution. Reworded to 'echoed in the US Bill of Rights'.
findings.evidence: text of the US Constitution and Bill of Rights

findings.claim: 'the People's Charter (1838) - British movements quoted American formulations directly.'
findings.truth: The six points came out of British radical tradition, chiefly Major Cartwright's demands of the 1770s. Chartists admired American democracy but did not quote its formulations. Reworded to 'British reformers pointed to the American example'.
findings.evidence: origins of the six points in British radical demands from 1776 onwards

findings.claim: '1976 Sex Discrimination Act' in a factors-essay mark scheme.
findings.truth: The Sex Discrimination Act was 1975; 1976 is the Race Relations Act. Lesson 11 already dates it correctly.
findings.evidence: Sex Discrimination Act 1975; Race Relations Act 1976

findings.claim: "Doreen Lawrence's eighteen-year campaign forced the Macpherson inquiry into existence" (also in a lesson 14 mark scheme).
findings.truth: Stephen Lawrence was murdered in April 1993 and Jack Straw ordered the inquiry on 31 July 1997 - a campaign of about four years. Eighteen years would take it past the 2012 convictions.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Murder of Stephen Lawrence': inquiry ordered 31 July 1997, report February 1999

findings.claim: 'For the top band on a 16-mark factors essay, AQA requires ... examples drawn from at least two of the four parts of the course', with the same rule in two knowledge checks.
findings.truth: The spec says the essay 'will target all four parts of the specified content'. It sets no two-part minimum. Reframed as teaching advice with the spec's own statement given alongside it.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, note on question 4: 'The question will target all four parts of the specified content.'

findings.claim: Lesson 1 questions 2 and 6 and lesson 14 question 6 ask students to 'Explain the significance of the seven factors framework' and 'Explain the significance of judgement, rather than listing, in answering the 16-mark factors essay'.
findings.truth: The significance question targets a key event, person, group or development from the option content, so these three can never be set as exam questions. Two options: (a) replace them with real historical significance stems and rebuild three mark schemes; (b) keep them but relabel the type as an exam-technique drill so students do not read them as exam questions. Recommend (b) - the drills are useful revision and the unit already carries full historical coverage of all four parts. Not edited pending a decision.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, note on question 2: significance 'of a key event, person/group or development ... from Part one, two, three or four of the specified content'
findings.ruling: Relabel the three toolkit questions as exam-technique drills in the relabel queue; not rebuilt here.

findings.claim: The unit contains no source-utility practice at all: zero of the 84 practice questions are 'How useful is Source A', and no sources appear anywhere in the fourteen lessons.
findings.truth: Question 1 of Section A is an 8-mark source question, a fifth of the section, and it can target any of the four parts. The gap is now named in the lesson 1 teaching text, but there is nothing to practise on. Two options: (a) commission a source pass that uses genuine, verifiable extracts (Magna Carta clauses, the Anonimalle Chronicle, the Pontefract articles, Putney, the People's Charter, Hansard, the Scarman Report) with real provenance; (b) leave the gap. Recommend (a) as a separate job - composing sixteen sources inside a fact-check would risk fabricating provenance, which is exactly what this programme is meant to remove.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, note on question 1: 'The source will either be visual eg cartoons, or written eg diary extracts.'
findings.ruling: No source-utility practice in the unit: separate source pass on genuine extracts (source-bank rebuild), not composed inside a fact-check.

findings.claim: 'the troopship Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury carrying 492 Caribbean passengers, most of them Jamaican.'
findings.truth: 492 is the traditional figure. The passenger list records 1,027 passengers, of whom about 802 gave a Caribbean island as their last country of residence. Left as 492 because that is the figure in every GCSE textbook and in the board's own resources; changing it alone would put the lesson out of step with the mark scheme.
findings.evidence: National Archives Windrush passenger list (BT 26/1237)

findings.claim: 'the boy-king rode forward and shouted, according to chronicler Jean Froissart, "You shall have no captain but me."'
findings.truth: The Smithfield exchange survives in several chronicles with different wording; the Anonimalle Chronicle is usually the source given for this formula, Froissart's version differs. The attribution is not secure but is defensible, so it is left as it stands.
findings.evidence: Anonimalle Chronicle and Froissart both record Smithfield in different terms

findings.claim: 'Trade union membership halved between 1979 and 2000, from around 13 million to 6.7 million.'
findings.truth: 13.2 million is total union membership in 1979; 6.7 million is TUC-affiliated membership in 2000. Total membership in 2000 was about 7.8 million. Either series shows roughly a halving, so the claim stands, but the two figures come from different series.
findings.evidence: TUC affiliated membership series vs total UK trade union membership series

findings.claim: Robert Aske was 'hanged in chains from the city walls' at York.
findings.truth: He was hanged in chains from a tower of York Castle (Clifford's Tower) on 12 July 1537, not from the city walls.
findings.evidence: accounts of Aske's execution, York, 12 July 1537

findings.claim: 'By 1263 the country was in open civil war, the Second Barons' War', while the same lesson's glossary dates that war 1264-67.
findings.truth: Armed conflict did break out in 1263, but the war is conventionally dated 1264-67. The lesson contradicts itself by one year.
findings.evidence: Second Barons' War, conventionally 1264-1267

findings.claim: 'Lord Shaftesbury - an evangelical Tory MP - led the Ten Hours Movement'; the glossary calls him 'Lord Anthony Ashley Cooper (1801-1885)'.
findings.truth: During the 1833-47 campaigns he was styled Lord Ashley; he became the 7th Earl of Shaftesbury in 1851, and his surname was Ashley-Cooper. Textbooks use 'Shaftesbury' throughout, so this is left alone.
findings.evidence: Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 7th Earl of Shaftesbury, succeeded 1851

summary: No lesson was clean: the unit teaches the wrong question set for Paper 2 Section A in every lesson, tariffing the comparison question at 4 marks instead of 8, teaching an 'explain a development' question the paper does not set, and omitting the 8-mark source question entirely. On top of that systemic error there are four further HIGH errors of fact: the 1381 London sequence, Chartists 'citing' a Putney text not rediscovered until 1890, Britain having a smaller population than the colonies, and John Frost cast as the prisoner the Newport marchers set out to free. 199 edits fix 34 findings; two items need Tom's call and six are recorded as notes.
